column4: God judges and no one can reverse or review His judgment, then the ayah names Him swift in account; the Judge's decision is both final and answerable to no higher court.
The Prophet says the Lord will gather the two sides and decide between them in truth, calling Him the knowing Decider; gathering, knowledge, and just settlement meet in one answer.
During the inhabitants of the Fire's dispute, the arrogant say that God has already judged between the servants; the verdict has become an irreversible condition shared by both parties.
God decides in truth, while the beings invoked besides Him cannot decide anything; sole worship and sole effective judgment are distinguished from powerless rivals.
When God's command comes, the matter is decided in truth and falsifiers lose; the arrival of judgment turns contested claims into a settled outcome.
Every community has a messenger, and when its messenger comes the people are judged equitably without injustice; witness, decision, and the prevention of ظلم form one scene.
A marital breach calls for an arbiter from each family, and sincere desire for reconciliation receives God's aid; human حكم is explicitly a restraint exercised for إصلاح.
Compensation for deliberately hunted game is assessed by two just persons; judgment measures a corrective due rather than giving appetite free rein.

People are forbidden to pass wealth to rulers or judges in order to consume others' property sinfully; corrupted judgment produces the injustice that the section's root account says حكم should prevent.
Two litigants ask David to judge between them in truth, without exceeding justice, and to guide them to an even path; the parties themselves state the proper work of a judge.
One litigant describes the other's ninety-nine ewes and demand for his single ewe, supplying the concrete imbalance the requested judgment must correct.
David identifies the demand for the single ewe as wrongdoing, then realizes that he has been tested and turns back repentantly; judging another becomes a check upon the judge himself.
God sends the Book and wisdom to the Prophet and teaches him what he did not know in the context of protecting him from a partisan misjudgment; wisdom and revealed knowledge secure the true verdict.
No soul bears another's burden; all return to their Lord, who tells them the truth about their disputes, joining individual responsibility, return, and final clarification.
The speaking skins say that God created people the first time and that they are returned to Him; first formation and bodily testimony converge at the return.
إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَىٰ places return to the Lord directly against the human transgression born of imagining oneself self-sufficient.
Every soul tastes death, is tested by evil and good, and is returned to God; the whole moral trial is bounded by the return to its Judge.
Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, making death the unavoidable passage to the return developed by the section.
Deniers claim they will not be raised, and the Prophet is commanded to answer "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّي" before saying they will be told their deeds; affirmation, resurrection, and account are explicit.
Those who deny the Hour are answered "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّي لَتَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ" by the Knower of the unseen; the yes required by denial is backed by exhaustive divine knowledge.
The Hour comes so that believers may be recompensed for their deeds, supplying the judicial purpose of the emphatic "بَلَىٰ" in 34:3.
People swear that God will not raise the dead, and the denial is answered "بَلَىٰ" as a binding true promise; the self-answering logic concerns resurrection directly.
Resurrection will clarify what people disputed and make deniers know their falsehood, adding adjudication to the raising affirmed in 16:38.
Immediately after the cry "This is the Day of dīn," the day is identified as the Day of Decision that they denied; dīn is thus glossed by enacted separation and verdict.
After naming God owner of the Day of dīn, the worshipers say that they worship Him alone and seek His aid; the Judge and the worshiped one are contiguous in the prayer's own voice.
God declares that there is no deity but Him and commands Moses to worship Him, establishing the sole worshiped one before the next ayah announces recompense.
The Hour is coming so every soul may be repaid for what it strives; it completes 20:14's sole worship with the same God's role as final Judge.
The one God promises to gather everyone on the doubtless Resurrection Day and asks who is truer in speech; sole deity, gathering, and a question demanding assent coincide.
God makes the earth and sky, forms people and makes their forms good, provides for them, and is proclaimed Lord; excellent formation grounds the worship commanded at the ayah's close.
The Living one, with no deity besides Him, is to be called upon with dīn made sincere; the worshiped Living Lord is the one before whom the section pictures creation standing.
God, the angels, and people of knowledge testify that there is no deity but Him while He upholds justice; sole worship, knowledge, and the maintenance of equity meet in one formulation.
When all are exposed, the question "Whose is the kingdom today?" is answered: God's, the One, the Subduer; ownership and universal subjection frame the recompense of the next ayah.
Messengers, scripture, and the balance are sent so people may uphold justice; revealed order equips humanity to perform the corrective purpose ascribed to judgment.
God sends the Book in truth and the balance, then warns that the Hour may be near; measured justice and final judgment are placed side by side.
The weighing on that day is declared true, and heavy scales identify the successful; the Judge's decision is represented as exact measurement.
After the courtroom scene of 39:69, every soul is paid fully for what it did, and God knows their deeds best; the verdict becomes precise recompense.
Angels surround the Throne praising their Lord after judgment is concluded in truth; the courtroom sequence closes by affirming the justice of its Judge.
Do they not think that they will be raised? is a negative question exposing the premise behind fraudulent measure and preparing the standing scene of 83:6.
The raising just asked about is "for a tremendous day," supplying the temporal bridge to humanity's standing before the Lord in 83:6.
Before recounting human formation, the surah asks whether the human thinks he will be left without purpose or obligation; creation is thereby directed toward accountability.
The human is asked whether he thinks God will not assemble his bones, making bodily resurrection the denied claim under examination.
بَلَىٰ answers the bone question and says God can restore even the fingertips; exact recreation supplies another Quranic model of affirmative response to denial.
Does he not know that God sees? uses a negative question to force acknowledgment of the knowledge that makes transgression accountable.
God asks whether first creation wearied Him and identifies the real problem as doubt about a new creation; the rhetorical question makes origination evidence for return.
People are asked whether they see how God begins creation and repeats it, and are told that repetition is easy for Him; first creation directly warrants resurrection.
Travel through the earth is commanded to observe how creation began, after which God produces the final creation; reflective knowledge of origins leads to the afterlife.
God originates creation and then repeats it, which is easiest for Him, and He is the mighty, wise one; recreative power and wisdom belong to the final Judge.
We created you; why then do you not affirm? opens a chain of questions turning bodily origin into a demanded confession.
The hearer is directed to the fluid emitted in generation, supplying the concrete beginning of the creator argument.
The question asks whether humans create that life or God does, forcing recognition of the creator before death and recreation are discussed.
God says that He has decreed death among people and cannot be outstripped, making death a measured divine appointment.
God can replace people with their likes and produce them in a form they do not know; transformation and renewed creation defeat human control.
Knowledge of the first creation is invoked as the reason people should remember, completing the passage's inference from origin to recreation.
Within the answer about reviving bones, God brings fire from a green tree; an experienced reversal makes re-creation less remote.
God's command when He wills a thing is only that it be, and it is; this explains how the creator affirmed in 36:81 effects the return stated in 36:83.
The creation stages prove that God is truth, gives life to the dead, and is capable of everything; the inference drawn from 22:5 is made explicit.
The Hour is doubtless and God raises those in the graves, carrying the proof from bodily and earthly formation into the judicial gathering.
People are asked whether they thought God created them aimlessly and that they would not be returned to Him; creation without return is rejected in a single question.
The response exalts God as the true King and says there is no deity but Him, joining the return of 23:115 to sovereignty and sole worship.
God makes everything He created good and begins human creation from clay; good formation starts a sequence that ends in return to the Lord.
Human progeny is made from an extract of lowly fluid, adding the bodily stage on which denial of renewed creation will stumble.
God proportions the human, breathes into him, and grants hearing, sight, and hearts; deliberate formation deepens responsibility for the faculties given.
Deniers ask whether, once lost in earth, they can be in a new creation; their real refusal is identified as disbelief in meeting their Lord.
The angel of death takes them fully and then they are returned to their Lord, completing the passage's creation-to-return movement.
Human striving will be repaid with the fullest recompense, describing dīn as exact payment rather than a vague consequence.
The final destination is to the Lord, joining the full recompense of 53:41 to return.
God causes both death and life, giving the agent of return sovereign command over both thresholds.
God creates the male and female pair, beginning a formation sequence parallel to the one behind 75:40.
The pair comes from an emitted drop, supplying the first bodily origin in that sequence.
The other creation is incumbent upon God, turning first formation into an explicit promise of recreation.
The Prophet is placed upon a divinely ordered way and told not to follow the desires of those who do not know; knowledge and law act as a rein on appetite.
God holds every creature by its forelock and the Lord is on a straight path; bodily control of the head supplies a close nonlexical analogue to the source dictionary's guiding bridle.
When the disputed right favors them, the same refusers come to the Messenger submissively; selective submission exposes desire rather than principled judgment.
The passage asks whether they have disease, doubt, or fear that God and His Messenger will be unjust, then identifies them as the wrongdoers; the divine court is explicitly cleared of ظلم.
People are presented before their Lord in rows and are told they have come as they were first created, joining origin, return, and appearance for judgment before the record in 18:49.
The condemned are stopped because they are to be questioned; physical restraint is exercised for an account, closely realizing the section's primary sense of holding back for judgment.
People come to God individually as He created them the first time, leaving bestowed possessions behind; first creation becomes the form of return and dispossession before judgment.
The revelation is sent as an Arabic judgment, and the Prophet is warned not to follow desires after knowledge; revealed حكم restrains appetite through knowledge.
The Prophet is commanded to worship God without associating partners, call to Him, and declare that to Him is the return; this supplies the worship-and-return frame for 13:37.
The delayed parties are appointed for the Day of Decision, a repeated Quranic name for the section's day of judgment.
What will make you know what the Day of Decision is? closely repeats Infitar's question about what makes one know the Day of dīn.
The Day of Decision gathers the present deniers and earlier peoples, turning the name into a universal courtroom assembly.
The Day of Decision is a fixed appointment, expressing the certainty and measured timing of the Judge's day.
The Day of Decision is the appointed time for everyone, another direct formulation of the final settlement's universality.
Everyone's return is to God, who then informs them of what they did; return carries directly into disclosure and account.
God knows the present state of all, and on the day they are returned to Him He tells them their deeds; exhaustive knowledge grounds the final accounting.
God is the subduer over His servants and sends guardians until death's messengers take a soul; this supplies the divine mastery and death scene immediately before 6:62's return and judgment.
God will repeat creation as He began it, under a promise binding upon Him; origination guarantees recreation rather than merely suggesting it.
The question rejects treating believers who do right like corrupters or the mindful like the wicked; final judgment must preserve moral distinctions.
No compulsion in dīn marks a boundary around the root's worldly subjection sense: the Quranic religion in this ayah is entered after truth is distinguished from error, not imposed as enslavement.
Shuayb's chiefs threaten expulsion unless the believers return to their community's creed, even unwillingly; coerced worldly return and subjection stand against waiting for God's judgment in 7:87.
The warnings are described as consummate wisdom, though warnings do not benefit the refusers; wisdom reaches the truth while leaving hearers responsible for refusal.
Moses says his Lord granted him judgment or wisdom and made him a messenger, identifying حكم as a divinely given capacity after his flight and return.
Does God not know best what is in the breasts of all beings? uses the same negative-question form to compel acknowledgment of the knowledge required for judgment.
Is the recompense of excellence anything but excellence? is a self-answering question that makes fitting repayment appear undeniable.

God is named creator, provider, giver of death and life, then the hearers are asked whether any partners do any of this; the question excludes rival objects of worship from the powers leading to return.
The hearers are asked whether they were created from nothing or are themselves the creators; the rhetorical alternatives compel admission of a creator.
They are next asked whether they created heaven and earth, with their lack of certainty exposed; the broadened creation question reinforces the premise behind resurrection and judgment.
The Spirit and angels stand in rows on the final day and speak only by the Merciful's permission, extending the section's image of creation standing before its Lord.
